rv.q: The idea of bringing families together, of reminding them that love and tolerance will see them through their problems, has to remain a key Broadway mission. Especially at the holidays. Especially when we’re all so battered by this persistent pandemic. Heck, comforting familial restoration is a public service right now.
Strange as it may be to say, getting shut down by the pandemic during previews last year might have been the best thing to happen to the new Broadway musical Mrs. Doubtfire.
The rest of the time, though, the songs dissolve into forgettability.

But it represents another in a long line of forgettable musicals adapted from superior films, which, in a nervous season of recovery on Broadway, doesn’t give a ready-to-cheer critic much to cheer about.

From a craft perspective, there’s a lot to like here, and it’s easy to get swept up in the moment and walk out with a huge grin on your face, as well as an appreciation for the staging and performances that went into the show.

This pleasant and forgettable show at the Theatre is the epitome of what Sondheim (citing his friend Mary Rodgers) called a “Why” musical: “a perfectly respectable show, based on a perfectly respectable source, that has no reason for being.”
It’s a wholly admirable, workmanlike performance: technically impressive if not charismatically embraceable.
Its musical counterpart feels unsure of what notes to hit, what jokes to rewrite and what updates to add to be relevant.

But even in the belabored tradition of screen-to-stage musical adaptations, "Mrs. Doubtfire" is doggedly risk-averse, opting for handsomely outfitted, faithful simulacrum over reinvention or surprise.
Alas, it’s a wholesome, family-friendly dud, and with a running time of two hours and 35 minutes, it’s too long to take the kids.

But in the context of rapidly evolving conversations about gender diversity, with real stakes for trans and non-binary people, the musical's central maneuver feels cheap, retrograde and like little more than a gimmick.

All the directorial panache Zaks brings to this lightning paced production, all the charm displayed by McClure, all the energy contributed by a tireless ensemble can’t disguise the obvious: Mrs. Doubtfire just isn’t worth the effort.

What we’re left with is yet another assembly line musical of a movie — an obnoxious one at that — in which every song by “Something Rotten!” duo John O’Farrell and Karey Kirkpatrick is generic and forgettable.
Mrs. Doubtfire is a winner that will delight audiences for a long time to come.
Mrs. Doubtfire is a silly confection, with a standard-issue heartwarming point.
Efficiency takes this “Mrs. Doubtfire” only so far.
All the ingredients are there, but perhaps some re-tooling is still necessary back in the kitchen.
The result is shiny, professional, and uninspired, a passable entertainment that struggles to avoid invidious comparisons with its predecessor.
But none of the theater makers involved seemed to have spent time answering the kind of basic question that Sondheim liked to ask: Why* does this need to be a musical?
The result? Over-the-top performances that are only flickeringly satisfactory on an emotional or even comedic level.

But while Rob McClure’s consummate skill as a singer, dancer, and comic actor represent a career defining performance as the eponymous character, a curiously dated aura hangs over the musical that no desire for nostalgia can quite overcome.

One hopes that future musicals that play the theater will be ones that at least make a good faith effort to live up to Sondheim’s innovative standards, as opposed to continuing the never-ending cycle of churning middlebrow musicals out of familiar movies.
Until then, I wouldn't recommend Mrs. Doubtfire unless you are able to snag a deeply discounted ticket.
For all of the calories burned, it's still low-impact.
That doesn’t turn out to be true, and I suspect (barring great word of mouth) the same fate may likely befall the show before the theater season ends.
The producers are lucky to have him but hardly lucky enough to make this Mrs. Doubtfire not come across more like Mrs. Doubt[mis]fire.
This is not a pale imitation, it’s a bad one.
This is pure silliness and McClure is genius at what he does, including voices and impressions, and probably has some Awards in his near future.

cn.t: Critics find this film-to-stage adaptation a professionally produced but uninspired cash grab that never justifies its existence beyond Rob McClure's energetic performance, with dated material and forgettable songs failing to escape Robin Williams' shadow.

sg.ra: SeatPlan and Headout consistently name Center Orchestra rows C-G as the sweet spot at this 2009 new-build Roundabout house, which was excavated up to 70 feet below street level to fit two-thirds of its seating on the orchestra level; the compressed footprint keeps C-G closer to the stage than most Broadway orchestras of equivalent row letter.

SeatPlan explicitly calls rows H-L the Orchestra's value zone, and Headout prices them around $115-120. A Sondheim-specific perk: row E was removed from the Left and Right Orchestra blocks, so SeatPlan notes row F (and by extension the H-L rows behind it) benefits from extra aisle-row stretch space. The mezz overhang does not start until around row K/L per BWW Forum and SeatPlan, so most of this band is still un-overhung.

A BWW Forum thread flags Left Orchestra row C as 'really really to the side - in an obstructed view sort of way,' and a TripAdvisor reviewer in Left Side Orchestra Row A during Beautiful reported the onstage piano blocked the right side of the stage while side-actor action on the left was cut off. Because the Sondheim auditorium was rebuilt underground in 2009 around the preserved 1918 facade, the side blocks wrap tight to the proscenium and are more angled than typical Shubert-era houses.

SeatPlan calls Center Mezzanine AA-BB 'highly prized for their unbeatable overhead views of the stage, perfect for watching a musical,' and Headout echoes that front-mezz rows are preferred over orchestra front rows by some patrons thanks to the elevation. The mezz is unusually compact here (around 328-357 seats) because the entire auditorium is an underground 2009 LEED rebuild designed by Fisher Dachs / COOKFOX with a steep modern rake, so even AA-BB feel close despite being upstairs.

SeatPlan credits the mezz's 'good rake' for letting patrons at the back still 'get a clean view down to the stage,' and Headout names rows CC and FF as value picks. Because the Sondheim was rebuilt to modern sightline specs in 2009 (Fisher Dachs, LEED-certified), there are no legacy pillars like older Shubert-era houses — obstructions here are angular (side mezz) rather than structural.
